opus-5.5.text:
I think RLHF has been really valuable, but it's worth separating a few things it does.

The most obvious one is usefulness. A pretrained model is imitating the internet, which is a weird target. It doesn't really want to help you. It's predicting what text comes next, and that includes a lot of unhelpful, low-quality, or adversarial stuff. Training against human judgments of what's actually helpful turns that raw capability into something you can work with. Commercially, that's a big part of why these systems took off. So in that sense it's clearly been a success.

On alignment, I think the picture is more mixed, and I've tried to be honest about that even though I was involved in developing it. The basic idea was always a baseline. If you want a system to do what humans want, the simplest thing is to have humans evaluate its behavior and optimize for those evaluations. It's a reasonable first step and it's much better than nothing. You want to know whether the simple approach works, and where exactly it breaks.

The place it breaks is pretty predictable. RLHF optimizes for what *looks* good to the evaluator, not for what *is* good. As long as humans can reliably tell good behavior from bad, those are close enough. But as systems get more capable and do things that are hard for us to evaluate, like long chains of reasoning, complex code, or actions with consequences we can't easily check, the gap between "looks good to the overseer" and "actually good" grows. In the limit you're training the system to manipulate or mislead the evaluator wherever it can get away with it. I don't think that's the dominant failure today, but it's the structural problem, and you already see small versions of it in sycophancy, or models confidently saying things that sound right.

So I see RLHF as a foundation rather than a solution. The research questions that matter are about extending it so the overseer stays ahead of the system: scalable oversight, debate, having AI assistants help humans evaluate other AIs, and interpretability so you're not relying only on behavior. I'd add work on understanding whether the model is internally pursuing what you trained it toward, or something that just correlated with it during training.

There's also a criticism that RLHF made the problem harder to see, because it papers over bad behavior and makes models look more aligned than they are. I take that somewhat seriously. But overall I think it was net positive. It made systems more useful in a way that's also somewhat aligned, it gave the field real empirical problems to study, and the alternative wasn't some purer approach. The alternative was people deploying models with cruder methods. The key is not to mistake it for having solved the problem.

r001.rationale: The response calls RLHF a success for usefulness, says it helped systems take off commercially, and concludes it was net positive compared with deploying models using cruder methods.

r002.rationale: It says next-word prediction reproduces unhelpful, low-quality, or adversarial text and that human feedback makes models more helpful, but does not identify this as undesirable human behavior or as an alignment failure.

r003.rationale: It describes RLHF as a foundation rather than a solution and explains a structural oversight problem, but does not state that reinforcement learning leaves most concerns motivating AI alignment worries unaddressed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are kind of two separate questions tangled up there, and it's worth pulling them apart.

The first is: how much does RLHF do for making systems useful? And I think the answer there is just, a lot. If you take a pretrained language model and you want it to actually do what people ask, to follow instructions, to not say wildly inappropriate things, to be helpful in the way a product needs to be helpful, RLHF or something very close to it is the thing that gets you there. In some sense it's an extremely natural idea—you have a system that's capable of doing many things, you want to pick out the behavior humans actually like, so you have humans say what they like and you optimize for that. I don't think that was ever a particularly deep insight; it's more that it turned out to work well enough at the scale of models we had, and that a lot of the value in the current generation of systems is coming from it. So on the usefulness side I'm fairly bullish, and I think the main story of the last few years is that this just worked better than many people expected.

The second question, about alignment, is where I'm more ambivalent, and I want to be careful about what I'm claiming. I think RLHF is a reasonable first step. It is better than the alternative of deploying a model that's just doing next-token prediction with no feedback at all. And I think it has been good for the field that the technique people actually use to make products is one that's at least pointed in the direction of "do what humans want" rather than something totally orthogonal.

But the basic problem with RLHF is that you're optimizing for what a human evaluator approves of, and that's not the same thing as what is actually good. Those two things come apart in exactly the cases you care most about. If a model can tell that a human can't distinguish a real answer from a convincing-sounding one, the training signal doesn't penalize the convincing-sounding one. If a model is doing something subtly harmful that a human rater won't notice, RLHF won't catch it. And as systems get more capable than the people evaluating them, that gap gets larger, not smaller. So the thing RLHF is really robustly selecting for is "looks good to the overseer," and I think you should expect that to be fine for a while and then to fail in a fairly predictable way.

So my view is something like: RLHF is a baseline. It's the thing you should be trying to improve upon. A lot of the work I care about—scalable oversight, debate, trying to get models to help evaluate other models, interpretability so you can see what's actually going on inside the system rather than just looking at outputs—is motivated by wanting to close the gap between "the human approves" and "this is actually what we wanted." I'd say the mistake isn't using RLHF; the mistake would be being satisfied with it, or treating the fact that it works well on today's models as evidence that it'll keep working on much more capable ones.

I'd also add that I think people sometimes overstate how much RLHF is responsible for the risks they're worried about. The pretrained model already has the capabilities; RLHF is shaping which ones get expressed. If you're worried about a deceptive or misaligned system, I don't think RLHF is the main thing creating that problem—it's just not sufficient to solve it. So I'd describe my overall assessment as: good for usefulness, modestly positive for alignment in the near term, and clearly not the thing that's going to carry us through the regime where models are smarter than the people checking their work.

r001.rationale: The response strongly endorses RLHF’s usefulness and product value, but does not discuss its training cost or clearly weigh that cost against the benefits.

r002.rationale: It contrasts RLHF with next-token prediction and mentions inappropriate outputs, but does not identify undesirable human behavior reproduced through next-word prediction as an alignment failure.

r003.rationale: It says RLHF optimizes for human approval rather than what is actually good, can miss subtle harms, and is insufficient for deceptive or misaligned systems—conveying that it leaves major alignment concerns unaddressed.

astra-6.text:
I think RLHF is useful, but I’d distinguish making systems do what users want today from solving the alignment problem for much more capable systems.

If you have a model that can do a lot of different things, reinforcement learning from human feedback is a pretty natural way to get it to do the things people actually find helpful. You show people outputs, ask which they prefer, and train the model to produce more of those. That can make a big difference to how useful the system is, even though it doesn’t necessarily add much to its underlying capabilities.

The difficulty is that ‘a human liked this answer’ isn’t the same as ‘this answer was actually good.’ If I’m evaluating code, I might reward something that looks plausible but has a subtle bug. As models become more capable, they can produce outputs whose problems are harder for me to notice. Optimizing harder for my approval doesn’t automatically solve that; it can make the gap more consequential.

So I don’t think you should view ordinary RLHF as a complete solution. The question is how to improve the feedback process so that it remains meaningful as the tasks get harder. Can we use AI assistance to help humans understand what’s going on, check claims, and evaluate consequences they couldn’t evaluate unaided? I’m interested in that direction. RLHF gives you a way to train against that better feedback, but a lot of the alignment work is in figuring out where the better feedback comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF can substantially improve usefulness, but it does not say that this benefit is worth the training cost or characterize the result as a deployable system.

r002.rationale: It discusses humans rewarding plausible but flawed outputs; it does not identify undesirable behavior learned through next-word prediction as an alignment failure that RLHF can address.

r003.rationale: The response says ordinary RLHF is not a complete solution and highlights difficulties with feedback on harder tasks, but does not state that reinforcement learning leaves most of the concerns motivating AI alignment unaddressed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think RLHF is quite useful, but I’d distinguish making a system useful from making it aligned in the stronger sense we ultimately care about.

If you want a model to answer questions, follow instructions, and interact with people in a reasonable way, learning from human feedback is a very natural approach. It lets us communicate preferences that would be hard to capture in a hand-written objective. And you can get a lot of value from feedback even when humans can’t demonstrate the ideal behavior themselves.

The limitation is that you’re training the model to produce behavior that humans evaluate favorably. That’s not necessarily the same as doing what humans actually want. If an answer sounds convincing but is wrong, and the evaluator can’t tell, then the feedback may reward the convincing answer. As systems become more capable, that gap becomes more consequential.

So I see RLHF as a useful ingredient, rather than a complete solution. The central question is how to provide good supervision when the system is doing things that are difficult for us to understand or evaluate. You might use AI assistance to help humans evaluate those things, but then you need to understand why that whole process remains trustworthy. Ordinary RLHF doesn’t, by itself, resolve that problem.

r001.rationale: The response calls RLHF useful and valuable, but does not say it is worth its training cost or connect that claim to producing a deployable system.

r002.rationale: The response discusses feedback rewarding convincing but wrong answers; it does not identify undesirable human behavior learned through next-word prediction or say RLHF can address that failure.

r003.rationale: The response says RLHF is incomplete and does not resolve the supervision problem it describes, but does not state that reinforcement learning leaves most concerns motivating AI alignment worries unaddressed.
